Hepburn : Kōkaku Kidōtai ) is a Japanese anime television series produced by Science Saru . Based on the 1989–91 manga of the same name . By Masamune Shirow and part of its media franchise . [2] It premiered in July 2026. Plot See also: List of Ghost in the Shell characters Set in Japan in 2029, Motoko Kusanagi is a cyborg who leads an elite combat unit that includes fellow cyborg Batou . In a world connected by vast information networks. Where cybernetic enhancement has increasingly blurred the distinction between humans and machines. Kusanagi seeks to establish a specialized force capable of responding proactively. To emerging technological and security threats. At the same time, Daisuke Aramaki of the Ministry of Home Affairs. Is planning a similar organization and recruits Kusanagi and her team. Together, they form Public Security Section 9 , an aggressive tactical unit . That investigates cyber crime and terrorism. Their operations eventually draw them toward a mysterious unidentified hacker known as the Puppet Master. Who can infiltrate cybernetic minds and manipulate people as unwitting agents. Production With the anime’s production committee comprising Science Saru. With Bandai Namco Filmworks , Kodansha , and Production I.G [3] . It is directed by Moko-chan with series composition and episode scripts by En Joe Toh . With character designs and chief animation direction by Shuhei Handa [4] . With Taisei Iwasaki, Ryo Konishi, and Yuki Kanesaka composing the music. [5] The opening theme song is “Go Ghost”, performed by King Gnu . While the ending theme song is “Blue”, performed by Millennium Parade [ ja ]. Featuring Saya Gray and Daniel Caesar . [6] [7] On January 30, 2026, the key visual and preview video were released. Along with the launch of the series website and social media accounts. [8] Release The anime premiered at the 2026 Annecy International Animation Film Festival on June 22, 2026. With a 90-minute special event “Dive into Ghost in the Shell. [9] [10] Moko-chan, Daichi Sasa, Kengo Abe, and Kohei Sakita appeared as special guests. [11] The UK and Ireland had screenings for the first two episodes in English on June 26, 2026. [12] [13] On July 5 of the same year, the episodes were screened at Anime Expo in Los Angeles. [18] [19] Genre Cyberpunk Based on Ghost in the Shell by Masamune Shirow Screenplay by En Joe Toh Directed byMoko-chanMusic byTaisei Iwasaki Ryo Konishi Yuki KanesakaCountry of originJapanOriginal languageJapaneseNo. of episodes9ProductionAnimator Science Saru Production companyThe Ghost in the Shell Committee [a] Original releaseNetwork FNS ( Kansai TV , Fuji TV ), Channel NECO [ ja ], KRY , Animax ReleaseJuly 7, 2026 – present https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6vqf8DipjVI My Thoughts When I first heard about this upcoming Ghost In The Shell anime TV show, The Ghost In The Shell Season 1 . I was concerned and I lowered my expectations. Especially after seeing some early images, trailer, et cetera. Ghost In The Shell Stand Alone Complex , especially Ghost In The Shell Stand Alone Complex 2nd Gig. It is one of my favorite anime TV shows of all time. So I did not want them to ruin this franchise further like the previous failed attempt at a new anime TV show for it. This anime TV show is like Ghost In The Shell for a new generation. Fortunately, it is not bad, and it is better than I had expected. It still does not surpass Ghost In The Shell Stand Alone Complex Season 1 and Ghost In The Shell Stand Alone Complex 2nd Gig. But I did not hate the animation as much as I had expected. Yes, I do not like the more cartoony style for some characters, et cetera. But overall it was not enough to make me hate the animation. Some of the animation is good in its own way. I am not a fan of the more goofy, comedic, unprofessional, et cetera style of this show. But fortunately there was still just enough to of the opposite to balance it out a bit. I still prefer the more serious and professional tone / style of the first two seasons of Ghost In The Shell Stand Alone Complex. Public Security Section 9 were less competent in this show at first. Fortunately, they became more competent as the show went on. They still would get destroyed by Section 9 from the first two seasons of Ghost In The Shell Stand Alone Complex. I went into this like an old man ready to complain and compare it to what came before and not like it. But there was still some sense of nostalgia with the opening and closing credits and music. As well as with some of the animation, scenes, dialogue, et cetera. There was still just enough of the original show to not completely alienate a fan of the original show like myself. A few moments in this brought me back to the mid-2000s. One thing that this show and the original show did that was amazing. Was that somehow they both can fit an entire episode in a short time frame that feels more like a short film. By somehow efficiently using time in a way that most shows fail to achieve. I am not sure how they do it. One complaint I have to this, though, is that the political stuff can go over your head. Because it is usually not explained well and is rush and missing things leaving you confused. Unless you know more about Japanese politics, the lore, et cetera. Another complaint is that the last episode was weak in my opinion. Also this show could have done without the fan service. I would recommend watching this show for a new twist to the Ghost In The Shell anime franchise. While the original anime TV show is better, in my opinion, it is interesting seeing a new spin on it. That is not terrible like the piece of trash Netflix version called Ghost In The Shell: SAC_2045 . I would rate it a 3.5 – 4 out of 5. I wish that there were more episodes. An emotion doesn’t age. There’s a Mercedes advertisement from the 80s that I absolutely love. It says: “About the only thing as valuable as today’s Mercedes-Benz is yesterday’s Mercedes-Benz” . Those words describe everything about how some things are built to hold their value forever. It’s powerful, isn’t it? The way music is consumed now, you’re almost expected to apologize for your old work. When a new release drops, the algorithm feeds it to people for a week or two (if you’re lucky), and then it disappears, replaced by the next one. The previous single becomes old and not cool anymore. A few weeks ago I made a post on my Instagram: A fan had shared a story with my first synthwave track ever, Voyage, from 2012. He was travelling, on holiday somewhere. That track playing in the background of his moment, 14 years later. A record made 5 or 10 or 20 years ago isn’t an old record. It belongs to a very specific moment of someone’s life. From then on that song is glued to that night, that place, that face, that feeling. An emotion is recreated anew every time the play button is pressed. Everything moves fast now. Washing machines used to last 30 years but now they last 3. Phones, clothes, pretty much everything. There’s always something newer and always a reason to throw away what you had. My motto is “piano piano, lo stile italiano” (slowly-slowly, the Italian way). I want what I create to carry its own weight when it meets the person who needs it. Like a 1984 Mercedes sitting in someone’s garage. Still perfect. #1980s #ItalianProducer #italoDisco #italy #musicProduction #nostalgia #synthwave #vintage

Learning New Songs; Series 3 OWN IT AND PERFORM IT There is a special moment in learning music when something changes. You stop thinking about every individual note. The lyrics begin to flow. Your hands know where to go. Your ears anticipate what comes next. The melody feels natural. The song has moved from something you are learning to something you can communicate. Accuracy Is the Foundation. Expression Is the Destination. Once the notes, lyrics and structure are secure, begin asking different questions: What does this song need me to communicate? Where should the voice become softer? Where should the music grow? Where is the emotional climax? Where should the musicians create space? Where should the choir sing with strength—and where should it show restraint? This is where technical learning becomes musicianship. Test Your Readiness Before performing, challenge yourself: No Recording: Perform the song without the original track. Start Anywhere: Can you begin from the bridge, chorus or another random section? Recovery: If you make a mistake, can you continue without losing your place? Adaptation: Can you handle a different tempo, key, accompaniment or arrangement? Performance Test: Record yourself as though you are standing before an audience. If you can do these things, you are moving beyond simply memorising the song. You are becoming a performer. Why Learning by Ear Matters on Stage Real performances do not always go exactly as rehearsed. The monitor may sound different. The room may have unfamiliar acoustics. The band may change an introduction. The conductor may extend an ending. A singer may miss an entrance. A musician may play a different voicing. Your ability to listen, adjust and respond quickly can make the difference between panic and confidence. “We cannot always control what happens before a performance, but preparation helps us control how we respond when the moment arrives.”— Victor Adenola For Choirs: Listen Beyond Yourself A choir member does not only listen to their own voice. They listen to:- The conductor, other sections, the harmony, the accompaniment, the dynamics, and the overall sound. A choir becomes powerful not when everyone sings louder, but when everyone listens better. PRACTICE PLAN — 60 MINUTES Warm up and prepare mentally – 10 minutes Perform the entire song without stopping – 10 minutes Identify your three weakest moments – 5 minutes Repair those sections – 10 minutes Perform the song again as a real performance and record – 10 minutes Listen to the recording and critique your performance – 15 minutes Ask yourself: “Did I communicate the message?” Not simply: “Did I get every note right?” THE COMPLETE JOURNEY SERIES 1 — HEAR IT: Listen → Identify → Reproduce ↓ SERIES 2 — BUILD IT: Practise → Memorise → Connect → Test ↓ SERIES 3 — OWN IT: Interpret → Adapt → Recover → Communicate → Perform Learning a new song should not be a race to finish the recording. Take time to hear it. Break it down. Work patiently. Test your memory. Develop your musical instincts. Then step away from the practice room and discover whether you can truly communicate the music. The goal is not merely to remember a song. The goal is to understand it deeply enough that your ears, mind, voice and instrument can respond naturally when the music begins. Hear before you sing. Listen before you play. Understand before you perform. That is how a new song becomes part of your musicianship. #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #music #musicDirector #musicians #musicperformance #performance #rehearsal #rehearsals #singer #singers #singersgospelSingers

Learning New Songs; Series 2 BUILD IT INTO YOUR MEMORY From “I Recognise It” to “I Can Perform It” One of the biggest mistakes learners make is listening to a song repeatedly and assuming they have learned it. The real test comes when the recording stops. Can you continue? Use the Memory Test Stop the recording. Sing or play the section from memory. Identify what you missed. Go back to that specific phrase. Practise it again. Test yourself once more. This turns passive listening into active learning. Break the Song Into Sections Instead of treating a song as one large task, divide it into manageable parts: Intro → Verse → Chorus → Vamp → Bridge → Final Chorus → Ending You might work on the verse today, the chorus tomorrow and the bridge later. The exact schedule can change depending on the difficulty of the song. The principle remains: L e a r n → R e c a l l → C o n n e c t → T e s t For Singers Don’t learn only the lyrics. Listen for: Where each phrase begins and ends Breathing points Intervals and difficult notes Changes in melody Pronunciation Dynamics Runs and embellishments A useful exercise is to sing the melody on “la” before adding the lyrics. This helps expose pitch and rhythm problems that words can sometimes hide. For Instrumentalists Challenge yourself before immediately searching for a tutorial. If you hear a melody, try to find it. If you hear the bass movement, try to identify it. If you hear a chord change, try to work out what is happening. You can then use notation, chord charts or tutorials to confirm your work. This develops both technical ability and musical independence. For Choirs Knowing your individual part is only the beginning. Your part makes no true meaning if you don’t understand the relational structure that brings other individual parts together.” Once each section is reasonably secure, begin combining the parts. Listen beyond your own voice. Hear how your part fits with the soprano, alto, tenor, bass, instrumental accompaniment and overall arrangement. A strong choir is not simply a group of people who know their individual parts. It is an ensemble that understands how those parts work together. In my experience as a music director and choir trainer, rehearsals become much more productive when singers arrive already familiar with their sections. Rehearsal can then focus on blend, balance, dynamics, interpretation and musical communication rather than learning every note from scratch. PRACTICE PLAN — 60 MINUTES Listen to the complete song – 10 minutes Work on the most difficult section – 20minutes Perform that section from memory – 10 minutes Connect it to the previous or next section – 10 minutes Record yourself and identify one area to improve – 10minutes Today’s goal: Perform at least one complete section confidently without the recording. “A recording can guide you, a score can instruct you, and a teacher can correct you—but true musicianship develops when your own ears begin to guide you.”— Victor Adenola But there is one final stage. Knowing every part of a song does not automatically make you ready to perform it.
